PART 7 — A Restoring God, Ignorance, and the Gospel of Union

Your question in brief. If God is restorative, and doesn't force but relates — then what of people, including Christians, who don't know this? Will He restore them automatically, or only if they come to the knowledge? If we don't turn to Him can we receive anything, even though He loves us and never leaves? Short answer: neither "automatically" nor "only if they first achieve the knowledge." God's initiative is constant and works before and beyond our understanding; what He restores is relational, so it is received in trust; and the awakening itself is something He gives. Details follow, with the places where Christians disagree marked.

7.1 The Restoring God: Scripture's Words

WordLanguageMeaningWhere
שׁוּב shuv (causative)HebrewTo turn back, bring back, restorePs 23:3 ("he restores my soul")
שִׁלֵּם shillemHebrewTo make whole, repay, make goodJoel 2:25 ("I will restore to you the years the locust has eaten")
ἀποκαθίστημι apokathistemiGreekTo restore to a former, whole stateMark 3:5 (the hand restored); Mark 8:25 (sight restored)
ἀποκατάστασις apokatastasisGreekRestorationActs 3:21 ("the time for restoring all things")
καταρτίζω katartizoGreekTo mend, restore, put in order, equip — used of mending fishing netsMark 1:19; Gal 6:1 ("restore him in a spirit of gentleness"); 1 Pet 5:10 ("will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you")

The picture is of a Mender, not of a Scorekeeper: God mends nets, restores souls, makes good the years. The question is how the mending reaches people who do not yet know the Mender.

7.2 God Present While We Are Unaware

SceneWhat it shows
Jacob at Bethel (Gen 28:16)"Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it." God was present before Jacob knew.
Young Samuel (1 Sam 3:7)"Samuel did not yet know the LORD" — yet the LORD was calling him by name.
Mary Magdalene (John 20:14-16)Jesus stands before her and she does not recognise him — until he says her name.
The Emmaus road (Luke 24:15-16)Jesus walks with them, "but their eyes were kept from recognising him."
Paul (1 Tim 1:13)"I acted ignorantly in unbelief" — and received mercy; Acts 17:30 ("the times of ignorance God overlooked").
Luke 23:34"They know not what they do" — ignorance is neither excused nor a barrier to God's mercy.

These are not footnotes: they establish that ignorance does not remove God's presence or stop His working. God does not wait for understanding to begin.

7.3 Yet Knowing Matters: The Two Sons

The older brother is the picture of the ignorant believer. He has never left; he has the whole inheritance within reach ("all that is mine is yours"); and yet he lives as a servant, keeping count, unable to feast. The father does not drag him in. He goes out and pleads (v.28), tells him the truth, and leaves the invitation standing — the parable ends without the older son's answer. Both sons were equally loved; the difference was in what each knew and received.

7.4 Three Claims, Held Together

ClaimScriptureWhat it protects
1. God's love and presence are constant and unearned.Ps 139:7-12; Rom 5:8; 8:38-39; Heb 13:5; Matt 28:20; Acts 17:27-28; 2 Tim 2:13 ("if we are faithless, he remains faithful")Against the fear that our ignorance or failure can make God leave.
2. God takes the initiative, before and beyond our awareness.Luke 15:4-7 (the shepherd seeks); John 6:44; 12:32 ("I will draw all people to myself"); John 16:8; Rom 2:4; Phil 1:6; 2:13 ("God is at work in you"); Eph 2:4-5Against the idea that we must first generate understanding to unlock God.
3. Experienced restoration is relational, so it is received in trust, and knowing matters.John 8:32; 14:20 ("in that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you"); Rom 12:2; Eph 1:17-19 (Paul prays that believers' eyes be enlightened to know what is already theirs); Hos 4:6; Rev 3:20Against the idea that restoration happens to people regardless of their response, like weather.

7.5 So Will He Restore the Ignorant "Automatically"?

GOD INITIATES — constant presence, pursuit, conviction, kindness
↓
AWAKENING IS GIVEN — "the Spirit of wisdom and revelation" (Eph 1:17); "flesh and blood has not revealed this" (Matt 16:17)
↓
THE PERSON RESPONDS — trust, turning, receiving (enabled, not forced)
↓
RESTORATION IS EXPERIENCED — peace, healing, freedom, communion; in time, fruit
  • Not automatic in the sense of bypassing the person. Relationship cannot be done to someone. Rev 3:20 knocks; Matt 23:37 ("you were not willing") shows resistance is real.
  • Not conditional in the sense of "only if they first get the knowledge right." The awakening itself is part of God's work. A person does not unlock God by understanding; God opens the eyes (Luke 24:31; Acts 16:14).
  • Security and experience are different questions. Many Christians hold that a believer's standing (Rom 8:1; sealed by the Spirit, Eph 1:13-14) does not depend on how well they understand. What ignorance typically costs is not God's love but the experience of freedom, peace and rest — the "orphan" living in an adopted home, or the older brother who never feasts.
  • God uses means. Scripture, community, circumstances, suffering, a friend's patient presence — God usually works through people and events, often without our noticing (Phil 2:13).

Where Christians disagree. This is a place of real, longstanding debate, and this document does not adjudicate the final scope of salvation.

Tradition (broadly)On God's restoration and human response
Reformed / CalvinistGod's saving grace is effectual: He regenerates and awakens those He saves, and they persevere; the believer's progress is certain, though means (Word, Spirit, church) are used.
Arminian / WesleyanGod's prevenient grace enables every person to respond; grace can be resisted; sanctification involves real, graced cooperation.
Hopeful or confessing universalist thinkersGod's restoring love will ultimately win every resistance — not by force but by overcoming (appealing to texts such as 1 Cor 15:22-28; Col 1:20) — held by some as hope, by some as conviction; others contest the exegesis.
Union / inclusion (Torrance-influenced) readingsHumanity's inclusion in Christ's humanity is an accomplished fact; personal participation needs awakening; writers differ on the final outcome for those who never awaken.

For readers of Kruger specifically: he is generally read as stressing that inclusion in the Father-Son-Spirit life is God's accomplished purpose and that the fallen mind does not know it. For his precise statements on the scope of salvation, consult his published work directly; this study does not attribute positions to him beyond the framework summarised earlier in the series.

7.6 "God Doesn't Force Anything" — Right?

StatementHow far it holdsRefinement
God doesn't coerce love, trust or communionFully. Love that is forced is not love; Rev 3:20 and Luke 15 show invitation, not conscription.—
God never acts forcefully in anyone's lifeToo strong as an absolute. God sometimes arrests attention dramatically: Paul on the Damascus road (Acts 9), Jonah in the storm and fish, Jacob wrestling (Gen 32).Say: God may disrupt and pursue, but He does not manufacture a person's trust.
If we don't turn to Him we can't receive anythingToo strong. Common grace reaches all (Matt 5:45; Acts 14:17); He sustains all life (Acts 17:25-28); He draws all (John 12:32).Say: we cannot receive the relational goods (rest, communion, assurance) without turning toward Him.
He loves us and never leaves usStrongly supported (Ps 139; Heb 13:5; Rom 8:38-39).Scripture also speaks of God "giving up" people to their choices (Rom 1:24) and of sin separating (Isa 59:2). The framework reads these as experienced distance and the withdrawal of restraint, not abandonment of love — a reading some Christians contest.

7.7 How the Gospel of Union Reconciles It

The key is to distinguish four things the Bible keeps distinct:

TermMeaningWhose actTexts
UnionBeing joined to Christ and, in Him, held in the life of the Father, Son and SpiritGod's accomplished actJohn 14:20; 17:21-23; Eph 2:5-6; Col 3:3; 1 Cor 6:17; 2 Cor 5:19
AwakeningComing to know and trust what is trueGiven by God; received by the personEph 1:17-19; Rom 12:2; Luke 15:17
CommunionShared life experienced: fellowship, rest, friendshipMutual1 John 1:3; Rev 3:20; John 15:4-5
FruitFreedom, healing, love, mature characterThe Spirit's work in a responding lifeGal 5:22-23; 2 Cor 3:18

Union is God's and unbroken; communion is shared and lived; awakening is the door between them. That is how "He loves us and never leaves" and "we must come" are both true: the first is about union and presence (always God's), the second about communion and experience (always relational). And note the grammar of 2 Cor 5:20: "be reconciled to God" (katallagete) is a passive imperative — an appeal to let yourselves be reconciled, to receive what has been done, not to accomplish it.

Where the analogy limits itself. A curtain is a poor picture of a person: people are not passive rooms, and awakening is not mere information. The aim is only to show constancy on God's side and reception on ours. The marriage picture helps in another way: a couple is married from the wedding day (union), but living as married (communion) is daily shared life.

7.8 What This Means for Helping Ignorant Christians

DoDon't
Pray Paul's prayer for them (Eph 1:17-19): that the eyes of their hearts be enlightenedShame them ("you should know this by now") — shame adds a curtain
Tell the story of what changed for you, and let them ask questionsArgue them into it; coerced agreement is not trust
Offer safe community where being known is not punishedIsolate them with correct doctrine and no relationship
Be patient: God is patient (2 Pet 3:9)Treat their ignorance as proof God has withdrawn
Remember you also have curtains you haven't seenAssume you've arrived

7.9 Case Study: Mathew, the Older Brother in the Pew

Mathew (composite) has attended church for thirty years, serves on committees, gives faithfully, and is worn out. Privately he believes God is "satisfied enough" with him when he performs and quietly displeased when he doesn't. He has never doubted the creed; he just can't feel safe. When a younger member receives acclaim, he feels a hot resentment — the older brother's "you never gave me a young goat."

What did not help. Sermons telling him to try harder; a friend who said he "needed to get his theology straight."

What did help. A small group leader, Daniel, who never lectured him, asked genuine questions, and told his own story of feeling like a servant in the house. One evening, they read Luke 15:31 together — "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours" — and Daniel simply said, "He's saying that to you." Mathew did not change overnight. But over eighteen months, as he was patiently known and still welcomed, the resentment softened; he began to rest on Sundays; and eventually he congratulated the younger member sincerely.

Read through Part 7. God had never left Mathew (claim 1). God was already at work — through Daniel, through the passage, through the quiet restlessness itself (claim 2). Restoration was received: Mathew had to say yes to a Father he had never quite believed in (claim 3). Nothing was forced, and nothing was automatic.
